report.source_text: One week after her initial presentation, she returned to the pediatrician's office with worsening symptoms. Though she had been taking amoxicillin-clavulanate as directed, the swelling on her right neck increased and began to have erythema and tenderness. She did not have fevers and was otherwise at baseline activity. Upon physical exam, she was noted to have right anterior superior cervical lymphadenopathy with overlying erythema. There was concern for inadequate antibiotic coverage or an underlying abscess. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was stopped, and she was switched to clindamycin to cover for possible community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. An ultrasound was ordered to further evaluate for a parotid abscess.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 4-year-old immunocompetent female presented with a right neck lump and abrasion (from a remote dog leash fall). Initial physical examination revealed right tonsillar lymphadenopathy and right neck abrasion. She was diagnosed with lymphadenitis and started on amoxicillin-clavulanate. One week later, despite antibiotic therapy, she developed worsening swelling, erythema, and tenderness in the right neck with right anterior superior cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound revealed a 2.2×2.0×1.5 cm fluid collection in the right submandibular region with heterogeneous echogenicity, anechoic center, isoechoic rim, and increased peripheral vascularity—consistent with abscess. Antibiotic coverage was broadened to clindamycin for possible MRSA. She was admitted for incision and drainage, yielding 5 ml of purulent fluid. Gram stain, fungal cultures, and acid-fast bacilli cultures were all negative. Bacterial cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) were not explicitly reported in available documentation. She was transitioned to oral clindamycin and discharged with complete resolution of parotid swelling and no further symptoms. The abscess was classified as idiopathic, supported by negative special stains and cultures, though the specific bacterial culture results and serologic workup for cat-scratch disease were not documented in available records.

final.trajectory_summary: A 4-year-old immunocompetent female presented with a right neck lump and abrasion (from a remote dog leash fall). Initial physical examination revealed right tonsillar lymphadenopathy and right neck abrasion. She was diagnosed with lymphadenitis and started on amoxicillin-clavulanate. One week later, despite antibiotic therapy, she developed worsening swelling, erythema, and tenderness in the right neck with right anterior superior cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound revealed a 2.2×2.0×1.5 cm fluid collection in the right submandibular region with heterogeneous echogenicity, anechoic center, isoechoic rim, and increased peripheral vascularity—consistent with abscess. Antibiotic coverage was broadened to clindamycin for possible MRSA. She was admitted for incision and drainage, yielding 5 ml of purulent fluid. Gram stain, fungal cultures, and acid-fast bacilli cultures were all negative. Bacterial cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) were not explicitly reported in available documentation. She was transitioned to oral clindamycin and discharged with complete resolution of parotid swelling and no further symptoms. The abscess was classified as idiopathic, supported by negative special stains and cultures, though the specific bacterial culture results and serologic workup for cat-scratch disease were not documented in available records.
